Appeals and Reviews

01 · Before you listen

A few words to know

Explore the vocabulary
false equivalence
Treating different things as though they meant the same.
discontinuity
A break in a sequence or pattern.
identifiable
Capable of revealing a particular person.
census
A complete count of a population.
substantiate
To support a claim with evidence.
opaque
Difficult to understand because information is not clear.

04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Emma's notebook had become an exercise in refusing false equivalences. Applications were not selections; selections were not payments; and the existence of a file was not proof of what it contained. Three columns offered a useful method, though they provided none of the totals she wanted.

Fiona Bell telephoned the next morning with an update from the records team. The surviving pages of the student travel reference list began at eleven and extended to twenty-six, with discontinuities. Emma asked the obvious question before allowing herself to be impressed: did the highest reference correspond to the number of applicants?

“I'm afraid we can't say that,” Fiona replied. “A number might have been assigned to an abandoned application. We haven't even established whether the sequence was continuous throughout the programme.”

Fiona was willing to share a descriptive inventory once it had been checked for personal information, but she could not release the identifiable list. Nor had the team located a complete record of who sat on the selection panel. The blank form's space for a decision indicated a procedure on paper; it did not identify the people who had exercised it.

Emma recorded the conversation as Fiona's account of a preliminary inspection. The documents themselves remained unavailable to her. She was becoming acutely aware of how easily second-hand descriptions acquired the authority of primary evidence when repeated often enough.

At lunchtime Sarah greeted the news with relief. “So there were at least twenty-six applicants.”

“Not established,” Emma corrected. “Twenty-six is an identifier, not a census. The numbering might include abandoned forms, or it might not begin with one.”

A fresh search of the newspaper archive produced a brief item from early October 2011. Several local students, it reported, were awaiting news of travel assistance. Neither names nor application statuses were given. Someone awaiting an initial selection decision and someone awaiting a promised payment might both have described their position in exactly those words.

Emma filed the article with its date and original wording. It supplied evidence that delays had been publicly discussed, not an explanation of their cause. It might be relevant to the parent's complaint about opaque selection criteria. It could not substantiate the anonymous caller's suggestion that payments had been improperly authorised.

She considered sending Fiona a forceful question about who had benefited. Instead she drafted a narrower enquiry: had the scheme provided for a review or appeal, and did any surviving policy specify how challenges were handled? She left it unsent while Fiona continued her inventory. Documentary requests were more useful when their purpose was clear and their assumptions were not embedded in the questions.

Shortly after six, Fiona sent a final message. One storage folder bore a covering sheet labelled “Appeals and reviews — Student Travel 2011”. She had not inspected the contents and made no claim that an appeal had actually been lodged. It might be a standard folder assembled in anticipation of challenges, or it might contain records of disputed decisions.

Emma compared the heading with the parent's published letter and felt a familiar temptation to join them into a conclusion. Instead she wrote two possibilities and drew a line beneath both. A process could exist without being used. A complaint could exist without ever becoming a formal appeal.

At the bottom of the page she added a question whose answer might prove more informative than another financial total: Who was entitled to challenge a selection decision, and what happened if they did?

She had not found the missing students. She had found the next document worth asking for.
